notes.title: Design diagnostic descriptions without turning logs into a protocol
notes.core: An informative object description improves observability but remains a human-facing diagnostic unless its representation is explicitly contracted. Expose typed accessors for programmatic consumers, keep cardinality and secrets under control, and distinguish a documented parseable format from a changeable summary.
rules: Override inherited Object descriptions for public domain value objects that need meaningful diagnostics.
Summarize huge object graphs rather than recursively dumping confidential or cyclic fields.
Document whether a string format is a compatibility contract; never promise stability accidentally.
When stable serialization or interchange is required, define a separate versioned codec rather than parsing a debug string.
Provide typed accessors even if the representation is documented so callers do not scrape it.
Preserve determinism where tests or log correlation need it, while avoiding secrets and high-cardinality identifiers.
nuance: Even an immutable record may generate a descriptive toString that includes secret components.
Record-generated representations expose component naming conventions but do not replace data-transfer schemas.
Lazy association traversal in ORM toString may cause extra queries or recursion.
A stable parseable toString format becomes a long-lived API burden once documented.
Calling toString in hot structured-logging paths can create unnecessary allocation and leak sensitive data.
notes.misconception: If a class has getters, consumers can safely parse its toString as a backwards-compatible machine format.
notes.production_context: A checkout audit event prints a masked summary of payment route and state, with structured event IDs supplied separately.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 records generate toString automatically, but generated output may disclose sensitive component values and is not a substitute for an explicit logging policy.

notes.title: Prefer explicit copying contracts over inherited clone machinery
notes.core: Java object copying requires a stated ownership model. Cloneable changes Object.clone behavior but does not expose a public cloning method; shallow copies retain mutable referents. For new domain APIs prefer constructors or factories that express which nested structures are shared, copied, or immutable.
rules: Treat Cloneable as compatibility machinery, not as a new generalized copy interface.
If legacy Cloneable is required, supply public covariant clone and restore independent mutable representation.
Never assume cloning an array containing mutable elements deeply copies the elements.
Use an iterative strategy for long linked chains to avoid recursive copying stack exhaustion.
Do not invoke overridable instance methods before cloned state has been re-established.
Favor copy constructors and conversion factories for newly designed value or collection APIs.
State identity semantics for unique IDs, locks, resource handles, and snapshot consistency.
nuance: Object.clone bypasses constructors, complicating final fields and invariant establishment.
Cloning mutable resources such as sockets or locks may not be meaningful or safe.
Arrays remain a practical use of clone for copying their storage, but elements can still alias.
A copy factory accepting an interface can choose different destination implementation.
Copying under concurrent mutation requires separate snapshot synchronization policy.
Java 21 records are shallowly immutable if components refer to mutable structures; record construction is not a deep-copy operation.
notes.misconception: Calling clone yields fully independent objects and always initializes invariants through the constructor.
notes.production_context: A risk rule snapshot copies mutable map/list containers while sharing documented immutable rule entries, avoiding aliasing between requests.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 records and List.copyOf/Map.copyOf offer concise defensive containers but are shallow, reject nulls in copyOf, and do not replace a deep graph-copy policy.

notes.title: Establish a coherent total ordering and test comparator laws
notes.core: A natural ordering is a public mathematical contract: comparison signs must be antisymmetric, transitive, and consistent when two values compare equal. Sorted collections interpret comparator equivalence as key equivalence, which may differ from equals unless intentionally documented.
rules: Implement Comparable only when one natural order makes semantic sense; use named Comparator for contextual orders.
Preserve sign symmetry, transitivity, and zero-equivalence consistency across all supported inputs.
Prefer Integer.compare, Long.compare or Comparator.comparing instead of subtraction which may overflow.
Compare significant fields in priority order and include meaningful tie breakers.
Define and test policy for nulls explicitly; Comparable instance method generally rejects null.
Document deliberate compareTo-versus-equals inconsistency and its effect on TreeSet and TreeMap.
nuance: Only the sign of a comparison result matters; avoid assuming a result must be exactly -1 or 1.
BigDecimal numerical comparisons treat some different scales as equivalent while equals does not.
Comparator.thenComparing can prevent equal-priority transaction records from being collapsed.
NaN, signed zero and locale-aware text sorting require an intentional domain definition.
Using a mutable field as a sorted-set key can break subsequent membership behavior.
Java 21 has established comparator-combinator APIs; performance anecdotes from older JDK versions require fresh benchmarks.
notes.misconception: An integer difference comparator is safe and TreeSet deduplicates entries strictly using equals.
notes.production_context: A payment ledger sorts by event timestamp and stable tie-breaker ID, avoiding silent loss of simultaneous events.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 Comparator.comparingLong and thenComparing remain available; records simplify value modeling but do not enforce ordering laws.

notes.title: Minimize exported surface and protect mutable state across module boundaries
notes.core: API accessibility is an architectural dependency decision. Keep implementation types and members narrowly scoped, export only deliberate contracts, and do not confuse a final reference with immutable contents. Module exports in Java 21 add boundaries, but classpath deployment and reflective opens change the effective access model.
rules: Keep top-level implementation types package-private unless external consumers require them.
Prefer private fields and only widen to package-private for a demonstrable collaborator or test seam.
Treat protected extension points as compatibility commitments rather than convenience.
Do not expose mutable arrays through public static final fields or getters returning original arrays.
Return defensive copies or genuinely immutable views whose backing mutability is controlled.
Document JPMS exports versus opens and test with modules where module encapsulation is essential.
Use public immutable constants only if the referenced object itself cannot be mutated.
nuance: An unmodifiable view of a still-mutated private backing list reflects later internal changes.
List.of and List.copyOf are unmodifiable but may contain mutable objects.
A public field in an unexported module package is not automatically reachable from external named modules.
Unnamed classpath code follows different access behavior from strict module-path deployments.
Reflection with opens weakens deep encapsulation; module metadata is not a full security boundary.
Interface implementation and method overrides constrain how far visibility can be reduced.
notes.misconception: public static final byte[] is immutable, and module descriptors make all Java code unreachable through reflection.
notes.production_context: A merchant KYC module exposes a validation interface but not writable static lookup arrays or internal token policy caches.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 JPMS has matured since the book described Java 9 modules as new; test exports/opens/module path assumptions rather than repeating era-specific adoption predictions.

notes.title: Avoid public mutable fields while preserving the right value shape
notes.core: An exported class with directly writable state makes invariants and future representation changes impossible to control. Prefer private fields with intentional access methods or immutable value records; internal package-private carriers can be simpler because their coupling is contained.
rules: Expose accessors rather than public instance data in exported mutable domain classes.
Validate invariants at construction and every mutating boundary, not only in getters.
Make accessors return safe copies or immutable values when backing fields are mutable.
Use a Java21 record for a public immutable data carrier only when its component types have safe ownership semantics.
Package-private and private nested internal carriers may expose fields when scope is truly local.
Recognize public final scalar fields as less dangerous but still representation commitments in an exported API.
nuance: Records publish accessor names and a component-based API; changing components can break clients.
Record components referencing arrays require defensive copies at entry and exit.
A getter without validation does not automatically protect invariants if a setter is unrestricted.
JavaBeans conventions and ORM frameworks may impose API compatibility requirements; weigh those before changing shape.
Package-private internal fields should not be used to transfer authority across trust boundaries.
A public record with a mutable collection is not deeply immutable without explicit ownership policy.
notes.misconception: A public final reference to a mutable array makes the array immutable; getters always make data encapsulated.
notes.production_context: A public merchant limit value provides validated read-only access, while private internal transport carriers use direct fields where safe.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 records supply concise public immutable-value APIs but are shallow unless mutable components are copied; do not blindly transpose 2018 getter advice to every record.
